{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_013f2YvK7S93k1bAmthzsFjU","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# AI / agentic layer — detail\n2\t\n3\tLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\n4\tdefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\n5\tis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\n6\ttreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\n7\tright after it, before any external exposure.\n8\t\n9\tAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\n10\thypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\n11\tconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\n12\trarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\n13\tA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n14\t\n15\t## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n16\t\n17\t### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\n18\tUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\n19\tall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\n20\timpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n21\t- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n22\t- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n23\t- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n24\t- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n25\t- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n26\t  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n27\t  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n28\t  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n29\t  design, not by filtering.\n30\t\n31\t### 2. Cost + latency budget\n32\tAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n33\t- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n34\t- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n35\t- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n36\t  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n37\t  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n38\t- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n39\t\n40\t### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\n41\tDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\n42\tirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\n43\tchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n44\t- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n45\t  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n46\t\n47\t## Capability order (build after defenses)\n48\t\n49\t### 4. Retrieval\n50\tGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\n51\tembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\n52\tpermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n53\t- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n54\t  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n55\t\n56\t### 5. Model access\n57\tA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\n58\tstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n59\t- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n60\t  at the stated threshold.\n61\t\n62\t### 6. Memory\n63\tWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\n64\tan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n65\t- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n66\t\n67\t### 7. Orchestration\n68\tHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n69\t- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n70\t  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n71\t\n72\t### 8. Routing\n73\tSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n74\t- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n75\t  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n76\t\n77\t### 9. Feedback\n78\tCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\n79\tretrieval tuning, or training data.\n80\t- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n81\t  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n82\t  poisoning path.)\n83\t\n84\t## Notes\n85\t- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n86\t  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n87\t  and eval scores — from day zero.\n88\t- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n89\t  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n90\t  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n91\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"791bc100-aeb0-415c-8f45-825aa8843822","uuid":"1d3e098c-b396-45bf-a6c2-d6bdc89e71f4","timestamp":"2026-10-03T00:25:20.365Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-core\\plugins\\p140aff59\\skills\\dependency-first-architect\\reference\\ai-systems.md","content":"# AI / agentic layer — detail\n\nLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\ndefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\nis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\ntreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\nright after it, before any external exposure.\n\nAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\nhypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\nconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\nrarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\nA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n\n## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n\n### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\nUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\nall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\nimpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n  design, not by filtering.\n\n### 2. Cost + latency budget\nAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n\n### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\nDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\nirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\nchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n\n## Capability order (build after defenses)\n\n### 4. Retrieval\nGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\nembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\npermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n\n### 5. Model access\nA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\nstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n  at the stated threshold.\n\n### 6. Memory\nWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\nan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n\n### 7. Orchestration\nHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n\n### 8. Routing\nSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n\n### 9. Feedback\nCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\nretrieval tuning, or training data.\n- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n  poisoning path.)\n\n## Notes\n- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n  and eval scores — from day zero.\n- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n","numLines":91,"startLine":1,"totalLines":91}}}

Classification and constraints\n- **What:** A scoring service in the authorization path that returns approve / step-up / decline / approve+alert, fed by streaming per-card features, with a loop that turns fraud outcomes into labels for retraining.\n- **Type:** Software, data infrastructure and a classical ML model (no LLM). Brownfield. Not a small build: it touches money, card data and customers.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Latency. Each decision must fit inside the authorization time window, and the decision must stay correct within that limit.\n- **Worst failure:** A bad model, threshold or feature change goes out to the whole portfolio and declines legitimate cardholders at scale within minutes. V6 guards against this. A close second is raw card numbers (PANs) leaking into the pipeline; V2 guards against that.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Scoring latency (round trip measured by the auth host) | p99 ≤ 50 ms, hard timeout 80 ms, then fall back to the existing engine | ASSUMPTION: a typical slice of an issuer's authorization budget before the card network steps in on its own. Authorization availability itself stays at the auth host's BASELINE because of the fallback | V6 |\n| Detection uplift | ≥ 10% relative gain in fraud value caught, at the existing engine's decline/alert rate | ASSUMPTION: the minimum that pays for the build. Compliance supplies it (dispute windows, audit), needed in Phase 1 | UNKNOWN | Phase 1 |\n| Run cost per 1k scored transactions | Ceiling UNKNOWN. Finance supplies it in Phase 1 alongside the uplift bar | UNKNOWN | V3 |\n| Operational complexity | 4 new runtime components (scorer, Flink job, online store, Kafka topics) and a 24×7 on-call rota | ASSUMPTION | Phase 5 entry |\n\n**Missing inputs:**\n1. The auth host stays the system of record for decisions, and existing case management for cases | The existing engine keeps running | V7, V9 | The existing engine's contract expires before V9 completes: re-plan as a declared exception |\n\n**R1 defaults:** online store is Aerospike (or Redis Enterprise) behind a feature-fetch interface; scorer in Java; Kubernetes with Argo CD; MLflow model registry; lake on S3 with Iceberg; per-segment decision-mode flags in versioned config.\n**N/A:** prompt+RAG vs fine-tune and hosted LLM vs self-host (no LLM); tenancy (single issuer, unless Missing input 2 says otherwise); data residency (pending Missing input 3).\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **Request:** a $1 card-not-present authorization on an issuer test card in the production test BIN range. A second test card is forced to score high.\n- **Path:**\n  1. The auth-host adapter (inside the CDE) tokenizes the PAN.\n  2. It calls the scorer synchronously over gRPC with an 80 ms timeout. The scorer reads one feature (transaction count per token) from the online store and applies a constant rule.\n  3. The response is logged by the auth host and ignored, because the mode is \"shadow\".\n  4. The scorer publishes the scored event to Kafka. A Flink job increments the counter in the online store, and a sink writes the decision log to S3.\n  5. The high-score card creates a case in the existing case-management test queue.\n- **Deploy:** Terraform for infrastructure; Argo CD for the scorer and Flink; the adapter goes through the auth host's own change process.\n- **Rollback:** Argo rollback for the scorer, and `fraud_scorer_mode=off` at the auth host, which takes seconds.\n- **Observability:** OpenTelemetry trace from the adapter through the scorer and Kafka (trace context in message headers) to Flink. Prometheus metrics for latency, timeouts, fallbacks and consumer lag, with Grafana dashboards and PagerDuty alerts. Logs carry tokens only.\n- **Who can reach it:** only the allow-listed test BIN range, and the scorer's output never changes a decision. Real cardholder traffic waits for V2.\n- **Also in Phase 0:** confirm the things that use the existing engine's outputs (the §2 rows); record BASELINES for auth-host processing time, peak authorizations per second, and the existing engine's decline and alert rates; start the organizational items (QSA, data-access approval, model risk, on-call staffing).\n- **Exit check (V0):** see §6.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Contracts and the PAN boundary**\n  - Unlocks: real traffic in shadow mode, the historical extract, and specifying features.\n  - Depends on: V0.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Event schema and identifiers (V1).\n    2. Harden tokenization and key management; deploy DLP scanners on topics, logs, traces and the lake; network segmentation; QSA review (V2).\n    3. Scoring API contract v1 with contract tests.\n    4. Extract 12–24 months of history through the same tokenizer into Iceberg, with point-in-time correctness.\n    5. Finance and fraud ops confirm the uplift bar and cost ceiling; compliance confirms retention.\n    6. After V2, widen the shadow mirror: one BIN range first, then all traffic.\n  - Rollback: shrink the mirror back to test BINs. If DLP finds a PAN, stop and purge the affected topic or partition.\n  - Exit check: V1 and V2 pass; shadow traffic reaches 100% with the timeout rate inside the V4 assumption.\n\n- **Phase 2: Defenses and budgets in the authorization path, plus an offline feasibility check (two parallel tracks)**\n  - Unlocks: committing to build, and specifying the feature platform within the latency budget.\n  - Depends on: Phase 1, V1, V2, and the data-access approval.\n  - Track A tasks:\n    1. Hard timeout and fallback to the existing engine.\n    2. Kill switch.\n    3. Decision config as a signed, versioned artifact with two-person approval.\n    4. Per-segment circuit breaker on the shadow would-decline rate.\n    5. Validate inputs from untrusted fields (merchant name, MCC, device data).\n    6. Load test (V4).\n    7. Shadow-mode rehearsal of V6.\n  - Track B tasks:\n    1. Label pipeline: confirmed fraud claims and fraud chargeback reason codes, with label-maturity windows.\n    2. Offline baseline features.\n    3. Out-of-time backtest of a gradient-boosted model against the existing engine. Transactions the existing engine declined are evaluated separately, because they never get outcome labels (V3).\n  - Rollback: config revert. Nothing is live yet.\n  - Exit check: V3 and V4 pass; the V6 shadow rehearsal passes.\n\n- **Phase 3: Feature platform**\n  - Unlocks: online features that match training.\n  - Depends on: V1, V3 (build), V4.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. One feature-definition repo that generates both the Flink (online) and Spark (offline, point-in-time) jobs.\n    2. Online store with replicas.\n    3. Backfill long windows from the lake.\n    4. Missing-feature defaults.\n    5. Rebuild drill for the RTO.\n    6. Online/offline parity check (V5).\n  - Rollback: the scorer pins the previous feature-set version.\n  - Exit check: V5 passes; the rebuild drill meets the ≤ 15 min RTO.\n\n- **Phase 4: Model serving, orchestration and shadow champion/challenger**\n  - Unlocks: the evidence for going live.\n  - Depends on: V5, V3.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Model registry; signed artifacts loaded into the scorer process.\n    2. Reason codes.\n    3. Rules-plus-model policy: hard rules (e.g. blocked card) override; score bands map to approve / step-up / decline / approve+alert.\n    4. Score-drift monitoring.\n    5. Analysts review a sample of alerts that only the new model raised.\n    6. Shadow on 100% of traffic (V7).\n    7. Submit the model-risk package (V8).\n    8. Get the false-decline appetite from fraud ops.\n  - Rollback: pin the previous model version; it's still shadow only.\n  - Exit check: V7 and V8 pass, and the false-decline appetite is in hand.\n\n- **Phase 5: Live decisions, smallest exposure first**\n  - Unlocks: fraud-loss reduction.\n  - Depends on: V6, V7, V8, the on-call rota and runbooks.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. V6 rehearsal on live internal cards.\n    2. Exposure ladder, assigning cards by a hash of the card token: internal cards → 1% of one low-risk BIN segment → 5% → 25% → 100% of that segment → the next segments. V9 gates each step.\n    3. Then enable the step-up band for card-not-present through the existing ACS.\n  - Rollback: per-segment flag back to the existing engine within seconds; the breaker reverts automatically. Because labels lag, there's a 60-day review after each step, and a step can be rolled back afterwards.\n  - Exit check: V9 passes at every step, and the fallback rate stays ≤ budget.\n\n- **Phase 6: Feedback and retraining**\n  - Unlocks: keeping performance up as fraud patterns shift.\n  - Depends on: Phase 5 at ≥ 1 full segment.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Automated label maturation.\n    2. Analyst dispositions enter the labels only through review.\n    3. Scheduled retraining, then registry, then shadow (V7 method), then canary (V9 method).\n    4. Drift and attack-pattern alerts.\n  - Rollback: the current production model stays unless a candidate passes.\n  - Exit check: one retrained model is promoted end to end, with no manual steps besides the approvals.\n\n## 6. Methodology exceptions\nNone.\n\n## 10.
